question: What do tube settler modules add to a conventional sedimentation basin?
correctAnswer: Inclined tubes that shorten the distance particles must settle before reaching a surface
explanation: Tube settlers fill the basin with inclined tubes, so a particle only has to settle a short distance before it lands on a tube wall and slides down. The basin itself is not deepened and no air or scrapers are added.
options: Additional basin depth for sludge storage
Inclined tubes that shorten the distance particles must settle before reaching a surface
Mechanical scrapers that push sludge to the hoppers
Aeration that floats solids to the surface
sourceTitle: US EPA: Surface Water Treatment Rules — supporting treatment resources
sourceReference: Supporting resource category: Enhanced sedimentation performance. See SOURCES.md: these are not claim-level verification citations.
optionA: Additional basin depth for sludge storage
optionB: Inclined tubes that shorten the distance particles must settle before reaching a surface

optionD: Aeration that floats solids to the surface

question: Why can a basin fitted with plate settlers treat more flow than a plain basin with the same footprint?
correctAnswer: The plates add a large effective settling surface area inside the same footprint
explanation: Settling capacity depends on effective surface area, not basin volume. Inclined plates stack many settling surfaces into the existing footprint, so the basin can carry a higher loading.
options: The plates heat the water so particles settle faster
The plates disinfect the water as it passes
The plates add a large effective settling surface area inside the same footprint
The plates make the basin deeper
sourceTitle: US EPA - Surface Water Treatment Rule Turbidity Guidance Manual
sourceReference: Supporting resource category: Enhanced sedimentation performance. See SOURCES.md: these are not claim-level verification citations.

optionD: The plates make the basin deeper

question: At about what angle from horizontal are tube settlers usually installed so that settled solids slide off the tubes?
correctAnswer: About 60 degrees
explanation: Tube modules are typically set at about 60 degrees from horizontal. That slope is steep enough for collected solids to slide down into the sludge zone, but shallow enough to keep the settling benefit.
options: About 15 degrees
About 30 degrees
About 90 degrees, fully vertical
About 60 degrees

question: Where do solids that collect on tube settler surfaces end up?
correctAnswer: They slide down the tubes into the sludge zone below
explanation: Solids land on the lower wall of each inclined tube, build up, and slide down into the sludge blanket below the modules, where normal sludge removal takes them away.
options: They are carried over the effluent weirs
They slide down the tubes into the sludge zone below
They are backwashed onto the filters
They dissolve back into the settled water

question: Which change most directly reduces the performance of an enhanced sedimentation basin?
correctAnswer: Raising the flow well above the design surface loading
explanation: Tube and plate settlers are rated by surface loading. Pushing flow well above the design loading shortens detention and carries floc over the weirs, no matter how well the basin is otherwise maintained.

Cleaning the effluent launders
Raising the flow well above the design surface loading
Recording the sludge blanket depth each shift

question: A filter run ends early because head loss builds up very quickly, while the effluent turbidity stays low. What is the most likely cause?
correctAnswer: Surface clogging of the media from high influent solids
explanation: Rapid head loss with good effluent quality points to solids straining out at the media surface instead of penetrating the bed. Heavy influent solids mat the surface and choke the run.
options: Loss of media through the underdrain
A broken effluent turbidity meter
Surface clogging of the media from high influent solids
Backwash water that is too warm

question: What causes air binding in a gravity filter?
correctAnswer: Dissolved air coming out of solution in the media when the pressure in the bed drops below atmospheric
explanation: When the head over the media is low, pressure inside the bed can fall below atmospheric and dissolved gases come out of solution as bubbles. The trapped air blocks pores and adds to head loss, which is air binding.
options: Dissolved air coming out of solution in the media when the pressure in the bed drops below atmospheric
Air leaking in through the backwash pump seals
Too much chlorine in the filter influent
Very cold water entering the filter
sourceTitle: US EPA - Surface Water Treatment Rule Turbidity Guidance Manual

question: During backwash, one corner of a filter bed boils violently while the rest of the bed barely moves. What does this suggest?

Media that is too new to fluidize evenly

question: What is the main reason a drinking water system chooses chloramine as its secondary disinfectant?
correctAnswer: It lasts much longer in the distribution system and forms fewer regulated by-products than free chlorine
explanation: Chloramine is a weaker but far more persistent disinfectant than free chlorine, so it holds a residual to the far ends of large systems. It also reacts more slowly with organic matter, forming fewer trihalomethanes and haloacetic acids.
options: It disinfects much faster than free chlorine
It lasts much longer in the distribution system and forms fewer regulated by-products than free chlorine
It removes hardness from the water
It does not need to be monitored

About 5 to 1

Shorter time between chlorination and consumption
Warmer water and longer time between chlorination and consumption
Lower precursor levels in the finished water

question: Why should filter run length and head loss be trended together rather than separately?
correctAnswer: Together they separate rising solids loading from media condition problems, which need different responses
explanation: Short runs with fast head loss growth suggest heavy loading, while short runs at normal head loss suggest a media or backwash problem. Either trend alone cannot tell the two apart, so they are read together.

Because only one chart is allowed per filter
Because head loss cannot be measured directly
